idiom_name: Akka ask with an implicit Timeout / Await.result(future, duration)
implementation_notes: Scala has no language-level timeout; the ecosystem supplies two library forms. Akka's ask (or the symbolic ?) requires an implicit akka.util.Timeout and fails the returned Future with a TimeoutException when the reply does not arrive, which is the standard way to bound an actor request; Await.result(future, duration) is the documented blocking form and throws TimeoutException when the budget expires. Pure-Future code implements the same thing by racing the operation against a delayed failed Promise (Future.firstCompletedOf). In all three shapes the timeout ends the wait but does not cancel the computation - Scala Futures are not cancellable - so abandoned work still occupies its ExecutionContext.
code_sketch:
implicit val timeout: Timeout = 3.seconds
val receipt: Future[Receipt] = (payments ? (ref => Authorize(order, ref))).mapTo[Receipt]
receipt.recover { case _: TimeoutException => Receipt.degraded }  // ask timed out
// plain Future: Future.firstCompletedOf(Seq(receipt, failAfter(3.seconds)))
pitfalls: Await.result blocks the calling thread and can deadlock when it runs on the same bounded pool that must complete the future; keep it at the edge (tests, main).
ask times out the requester only: the receiving actor does not know the reply was abandoned and may still complete, or start, the work.
The implicit Timeout is resolved by nearest-implicit rules, so a local declaration silently changes the budget of the ask it wraps.
A Future that timed out is not cancelled: it still runs on its ExecutionContext, so a tight timeout on many calls turns into pool saturation instead of protection.
